This study investigates the nonlinear dynamics of solitary and shock waves within a magnetized, electron-irradiated, electron-rich, and dust-laden plasma environment. Employing the reductive perturbation technique, we derive the modified Korteweg-de Vries (mKdV) and non-linear Schrödinger (NLS) equations, which govern the properties of both solitary and shock structures. These waves are characterized by being either solitary or double-peaked. Our analysis reveals that the formation of these waves is influenced by the ion fluid temperature, the electron non-thermal parameter, and the ratio of dust charge to ion charge. Specifically, the observed waves are categorized as either dust-acoustic or electron-acoustic types.

This paper introduces a contrastive context prediction (CCP) task for sentence representation learning, which is designed to be language-agnostic and to leverage multilingual data. Unlike prior work that relies on task-specific or monolingual assumptions, CCP utilizes a masked language modeling approach to model the contrastive relationship between a source sentence and its predicted context. This method is trained on a multilingual dataset, enabling the acquisition of robust representations that generalize across languages. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across various downstream applications. Additionally, we evaluate the utility of these learned representations for cross-lingual transfer learning, achieving performance that rivals state-of-the-art multilingual sentence embeddings.

This paper introduces a new multimodal learning framework designed to overcome the challenges posed by asynchronous modalities. By leveraging the geometric properties of a multimodal embedding space, we propose a simple yet effective approach called PMR (Prototypical Modality Rebalance). This method dynamically adjusts the contribution of each modality during training, enabling slower sources to learn more effectively by leveraging the information provided by faster ones. The proposed approach is straightforward to implement and compatible with various existing multimodal learning algorithms. Experimental results on three distinct tasks demonstrate that PMR consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving improvements of up to 3.5% in accuracy.

We examine the derivation of the massless fermion Vlasov equation within the context of the curved spacetime framework, incorporating the divergence of the local particle number density to account for the conserved current. By applying the gauge-invariant Wigner function formalism, we derive the corresponding kinetic equations. Our findings demonstrate that the term arising from the divergence of the local particle number density manifests as a source within the kinetic equation.

This study introduces a novel command recognition framework that merges the capabilities of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). The proposed model, designated as CNN+(TT-DNN), utilizes a specialized architecture featuring a compact convolutional layer designed to extract temporal features from audio waveforms. These extracted features are then processed by a densely connected neural network to derive the final command recognition results. The efficacy of this model was evaluated using the 2018 DCASE Challenge dataset, specifically targeting task3b, which focuses on 24-class command recognition. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the CNN+(TT-DNN) model achieves superior command recognition accuracy compared to a traditional CNN model while utilizing significantly fewer parameters.

This study investigates the control of deterministic evolution in a quantum system governed by a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. We demonstrate that by applying a time-dependent external drive, it is possible to steer the system's trajectory to match a pre-defined path. The required external drive is determined by solving a non-Hermitian version of the Riccati equation, which is derived from the system's Schrödinger equation. We further prove that the resulting drive possesses a unique solution, ensuring the controllability of the system. Additionally, we examine the behavior of the drive's magnitude in the limit of large coupling strengths.

We introduce a novel plasmonic solar cell design featuring a back reflector made of a metal-dielectric-metal (MDM) composite. This configuration utilizes a thin dielectric layer sandwiched between two metallic back reflectors to generate surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) at the metal-dielectric interfaces. The proposed architecture is designed to enhance light absorption within the active layer by exciting SPPs at both the rear interfaces. The study evaluates the performance of this SPP-assisted solar cell using aluminum nanoparticles and a thin-film indium gallium selenide (IGS) absorber. The results demonstrate that aluminum nanoparticles achieve a peak conversion efficiency of 20.1%, surpassing the 14.2% efficiency obtained with silver nanoparticles. Additionally, the research confirms that the MDM structure functions effectively as a back reflector, successfully coupling incident light into SPPs at the metal-dielectric boundaries.

This paper introduces an algebra of binary relations that serves as a formal apparatus for representing and analyzing the computational aspects of dynamic systems. By synthesizing a binary relation algebra with linear-time modal dynamic logic, we achieve a framework that characterizes both the state transitions and temporal evolution of such systems. Our approach, which relies on a novel algebraic theory of modal operators, facilitates the formalization of dynamic system behaviors and enables the formal verification of their correctness.

Tensor decomposition (TD) has become a vital technique for optimizing the performance of deep neural network (DNN) inference. However, current TD-based hardware solutions often fail to deliver high efficiency, primarily due to their reliance on fixed tensor ranks and the use of standard matrix multiplication (MM) units, which struggle with the non-square dimensions typical of TD operations. To address these limitations, we introduce FDHT-LSTM, a hybrid architecture combining fully dynamic tensor ranks with low-precision, approximate matrix-vector multiplication (MVM) units. This design enables the system to adaptively determine the optimal rank for every tensor and every MVM block, thereby maximizing accuracy- and energy-efficiency trade-offs. Furthermore, we develop a novel hardware accelerator featuring a specialized approximate MVM unit that leverages the inherent sparsity of TD-derived tensors. The FDHT-LSTM architecture is implemented in a 16nm CMOS process, achieving a peak throughput of 10.2 Gops/s with an energy efficiency of 1.0 pJ/MAC. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed design outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives by 1.5x in energy efficiency and 1.3x in throughput, all while maintaining negligible accuracy degradation.

UAVs are increasingly utilized in diverse sectors, including agriculture, surveillance, and search and rescue missions. However, MAVLink communications are susceptible to interception and manipulation by adversaries. This paper investigates the security of UAVs, focusing on the encryption algorithms available for protecting MAVLink messages. We evaluated three methods: AES, RSA, and SHA-256. Our findings indicate that while all three algorithms effectively secure MAVLink messages, the AES algorithm offers the highest efficiency.

This paper introduces a novel methodology for deriving network emulation models by analyzing the impact of various modeling choices on the resulting formulations. It posits that certain model components inherently emerge due to focusing on end-to-to-end properties, notably simplifying the model by bypassing intricate low-level details. Furthermore, the work demonstrates how specific architectural features of contemporary networks lead to the identification of pivotal elements within the emulation framework.

The Newman-Penrose formalism, which represents the Weyl curvature tensor in terms of complex angles, was initially developed as a geometrically invariant mapping. In contrast, a twistorial formulation of this map, which relies on the choice of a specific null infinity, lacks this invariance. This paper demonstrates that the triality of general relativity can be utilized to construct an alternative, non-twistorial approach that remains geometrically invariant. This new method is derived by transforming the standard Newman-Penrose map into the language of spinors, followed by a re-expression of that result using the Einstein triad.

The Muon Telescope Laboratory (MTL), situated at CERN, is a 10-meter-diameter, 10-ton structure constructed from 1,000 tons of steel, serving as a unique environment for studying cosmic ray muons. This facility supports research in various fields, including geology, physics, and archaeology, with applications ranging from analyzing geological structures and particle interactions to investigating human history. Specifically, the lab has been utilized to detect cosmic-ray muons passing through the Great Pyramid of Giza, revealing previously unknown internal voids. Additionally, it has been employed to study the Han Dynasty tomb at Mawangulin in China and the Colosseum in Rome. This paper details the MTL's design, instrumentation, data acquisition, and analysis, while showcasing results from recent measurements of cosmic ray muon flux and angular distributions.

The Generalized LALR (GLL) parsing algorithm is a well-established technique for parsing context-free languages, offering a broader range of supported grammars than traditional LALR parsers. However, the original GLL algorithm is noted for its high memory usage and substantial computational overhead. This paper introduces PEGLL, a new GLL algorithm that maintains the capability to handle complex grammars found in real-world languages while significantly reducing both time and space costs. The proposed method leverages the concept of a "reduced parse tree," which is derived from the abstract syntax tree generated by an attribute grammar compiler. By utilizing this structure, PEGLL eliminates the need for a parse stack, manages recursive grammar rules, and effectively detects semantic actions. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through its application to the C language, with experimental results showing that it surpasses existing state-of-the-art parsing methods in terms of both execution speed and memory efficiency.

This study examines the spontaneous radiative decay of a massive scalar particle into a fermion-antifermion pair, a process that is thermally enhanced. We analyze this phenomenon within the framework of finite-temperature field theory, focusing on the radiation spectrum and its dependence on temperature and kinematics. The findings indicate that the radiation rate vanishes at infinite temperature, a behavior that persists even when the process remains kinematically allowed. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the differential rate exhibits a singularity at the specific energy where the emitted radiation is collinear with the outgoing particle carrying the largest mass.

This study examines how linguistic context influences the relationship between word predictability and surprise responses. We analyzed a large-scale corpus of 1,000 English texts to measure how surprise reactions correlate with the frequency of a target word, while simultaneously incorporating linguistic context by using a weighted average of conditional entropy values from preceding words. We hypothesized that longer linguistic contexts would yield stronger statistical associations between predicted word properties and actual surprise levels. Our findings indicate that expanding the context window significantly improves predictive accuracy, particularly for words with lower frequency.

This paper introduces a new approach to 3D object pose estimation that utilizes a multi-stage training scheme to enhance the learning of canonical poses. By employing a hierarchical process that progressively refines predictions from coarse to fine details, our method effectively captures fine-grained features while preventing overfitting. We evaluate our framework on the 3D Object Detection Network (3D-ODN) benchmark, demonstrating that it outperforms the state-of-the-art.

We investigate an $AB_2$ InSb-based semiconductor nanowire, which possesses a large intrinsic spin-orbit coupling, utilizing a two-dimensional electrostatic gate to create a tunable quantum dot array. Our findings indicate that the strong spin-orbit coupling in InSb interacts significantly with an external magnetic field, resulting in a tunable coupling between the quantum dots. This interaction arises from a magnetic-field-dependent modulation of the spin-orbit coupling strength. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spin-orbit coupling can be adjusted via the gate voltage, which alters the Fermi energy. Consequently, the system exhibits a magnetic-field-driven Kondo effect that can be switched on or off. This mechanism offers a promising pathway for developing spin qubits with long coherence times and for engineering nanoscale spintronic devices.

This study introduces a novel 2D simulation framework for radiation-dominated shocks that incorporates pitch-angle scattering. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional 2D models, which fail to capture the full range of particle energies observed in 3D simulations. By employing a Monte Carlo method to model the pitch-angle distribution, we demonstrate that the resulting high-energy tails align with those produced in 3D simulations. Furthermore, we examine the influence of varying scattering rates on particle energy distribution and shock dynamics, concluding that the rate of scattering is a critical parameter for accurately modeling the physical processes within the shock.

The precision measurement of the Higgs diphoton decay rate offers a valuable avenue for probing the Higgsstrahlung process. This study examines the sensitivity of the combination of Higgsstrahlung and the diphoton final state to detecting new heavy neutral scalars within extended scalar frameworks. We demonstrate that, in the Higgsstrahlung production mode, new heavy scalars can be discovered up to approximately 1.5 times the electroweak vacuum expectation value ($2M \lesssim 2.5 v_{\rm EW}$). This reach represents a significant enhancement compared to the purely Higgsstrahlung channel, which is limited to masses below roughly 1.3 times the electroweak vacuum expectation value ($2M \lesssim 1.3 v_{\rm EW}$).

This paper introduces the idea of a joint numerical radius applicable to a pair of bounded linear operators. We establish several fundamental properties of this joint numerical nature. Additionally, we apply these concepts to solve problems regarding the best approximation of an operator $Z$ by the commutator of two specific operators. Finally, we derive multiple consequences and refine existing known results.

Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) and the Privacy Amplification by Time Averaging of Enclaves (PATE) are two prominent methods for deploying private machine learning. This paper evaluates their performance in financial domains, specifically focusing on credit scoring and portfolio optimization. Our findings indicate that DP-SGD delivers superior performance across all tested scenarios, whereas PATE proves more privacy-centric.

This study extends the general Wold decomposition framework for second-order stationary operators to multivariate second-order random distribution fields defined on $\mathbb{R}^d$. The proposed decomposition is demonstrated through an application to the stochastic $\alpha$-fractional Laplacian in a stochastic context, specifically within the framework of multivariate second-order random distribution fields.

This study examines the impact of dust and impurities on the ignition of a gas mixture using a laser. The analysis utilizes a one-dimensional model that accounts for the thermal and chemical evolution of the gas alongside the temperature dynamics of the particles. The results demonstrate that the presence of particles can either enhance or impede the reactive process, contingent upon their specific physical and chemical characteristics.

We introduce a Boundary-Aware Segmentation Network (BANS) designed to enhance the accuracy of semantic segmentation by explicitly modeling object boundaries. This approach utilizes a specialized Boundary-Aware Module (BAM) that integrates a boundary-aware feature map with the standard encoder-decoder architecture. The boundary features are generated by applying a morphological distance transform to the output of a dedicated boundary detection network. Experiments conducted on the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset demonstrate that BNS significantly improves results for both the "general" and "real-time" segmentation challenges. Furthermore, we developed practical applications based on this architecture, including a tool for segmenting the human body in images and a system for identifying road surfaces in aerial imagery.

This paper introduces the Driver-Messenger System (DMS), a framework designed to facilitate safe lane changes by leveraging a cooperative approach between vehicles. In this system, a driver initiates a lane-change request, which is transmitted to a designated "designated lane" via a mobile device. The system then evaluates the safety of performing the maneuver in the current lane versus the target lane and selects the optimal path. Simulation results indicate that DMS achieves a 100% success rate for lane changes, with no instances of collisions occurring during testing.

Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles (AOUPs) are modeled as Brownian particles driven by colored noise, mimicking the stochastic behavior of biological entities. This study examines the statistical distribution of such particles in proximity to hard-walled geometries, specifically examining flat surfaces, spherical shells, and hard walls. The analysis reveals that the distribution function for an AOUP near a boundary is governed by the first eigenfunction of the Fokker-Planck operator, a problem that can be addressed using the path integral formalism. By employing a path integral representation for the distribution function, the authors apply the method of images to solve for flat surfaces and spherical shells. Additionally, the distribution function at hard walls is derived using a variational approximation. These findings are compared with those of passive particles, highlighting the impact of the correlation time of the colored noise on the resulting behavior.

The electronic structure of the average atom model is typically solved using Siegert states, which represent a time-independent approach to the time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation. These states are defined as scattering solutions that are orthogonal to bound states and are essential for determining the atom's continuum density of states. This study evaluates the computational efficiency of Siegert states against the traditional method of uniformly partitioning the continuum into equidistant energy levels. The analysis compares both approaches regarding accuracy and numerical cost, specifically examining their impact on the calculation of atomic polarizabilities and ionization energies. The findings indicate that Siegert states offer a computationally efficient method for solving average atom electronic structures while maintaining high accuracy.

This study examines the Si IV line profile of the solar active region NOAA 12192, observed by the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS) on July 12, 2017, during a 1.2 flare. The analysis reveals a secondary component in the Si IV line with a redshift of approximately 100 km/s, which correlates with plasma outflows detected by the Solar Dynamic Observatory's Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager during the flare. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the secondary component's intensity increases alongside the Fe XIII line, indicating a shared origin for the Si IV and Fe XIII emissions.

Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) offers a compelling framework for understanding the universe's composition, particularly regarding its matter-antimatter asymmetry. This study examines QCD in the regime where the theta parameter exceeds zero, revealing a potential resolution to the strong CP problem when theta is precisely zero. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that QCD exhibits a novel phase transition at a non-zero theta value, a phenomenon that could manifest as observable astrophysical consequences.

The study employs molecular dynamics simulations to examine how ion irradiation affects the evolution of amorphous thin films. The initial amorphous structure was established by rapidly quenching a solid, while subsequent irradiation was conducted using ions with a range of energies. The analysis reveals that the interface relation can be elucidated through geometric arguments, specifically the competition between the minimum ion penetration depth and the film thickness. Additionally, the results demonstrate that irradiation-induced damage accumulates over time, with the number of displaced atoms increasing monotonically as the number of incident ions rises.

This article introduces a novel Router mechanism designed to safeguard source code against plagiarism by generating a unique output for every distinct input provided. The proposed method employs a pseudo-random number generator rooted in the internal file system architecture, specifically leveraging the characteristics of the code itself to produce varied results based on different inputs. The author demonstrates the Router's implementation in C++ and validates its efficacy through a series of experiments.

We establish that for the class $\mathcal{H}^\infty$, the abscissa of absolute convergence for Dirichlet series is at least $1/2$. This outcome is achieved by applying the method of moments to demonstrate that certain $L^2$-normalized Dirichlet series within $\mathcal{H}^\infty$ fail to converge absolutely. Additionally, we derive a more precise result regarding pointwise convergence by calculating the absolute moment of a specific $L^2$-normalized Dirichlet series belonging to the subspace generated by $L^1(\mathbb{R})$.

We demonstrate that groups with bounded exponent are contained within a specific bound-defined $k,r$-metric approximate subgroup. Consequently, we establish that bounded exponent groups possess bounded normal subgroup index, bounded size of their generating sets, and bounded generation numbers. This result further proves that groups with bounded exponent are virtually bounded generation groups.

We introduce novel algorithms for calculating log-concave maximum likelihood estimators, built on randomized and Nesterov smoothing techniques within the convex optimization framework. These methods are designed to be memory-efficient, capable of operating with only a single pass through the data. Furthermore, they are straightforward to implement, allowing for rapid execution on both standard computers and mobile devices. Empirical results indicate that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of computational speed, especially when processing large datasets.

The non-interacting rigid arch model (NIram) serves as a foundational framework for understanding the mechanical stability of granular assemblies. In this model, force transmission occurs exclusively through a specific set of rigid arches, where each arch consists of two particles connected by a single force-carrying bond. This work introduces a novel method for identifying such non-interacting arches in three-dimensional systems, which can be applied to both static and dynamic configurations. We demonstrate that the NIram is a valid approximation for stable states in a wide range of three-dimensional granular packings. Furthermore, we establish that the model accurately predicts the fluctuations in stress and force within the system.

This paper examines a two-player game played on a directed graph, where two participants take turns traversing a subset of its vertices. Movement is constrained to edges connecting the current node to an adjacent one. Victory is achieved by a player who visits the maximum number of vertices during the game. Optimal play is guaranteed to visit no more than $|V|$ vertices, where $n$ represents the total count of vertices in the graph. We introduce a dynamic programming algorithm with a time complexity of $O(n^3)$ to determine the minimum vertex count reachable under optimal strategy. Additionally, we present a randomized algorithm with $O(n^2)$ complexity that generates a solution with a 2-approximation guarantee for this problem.

The spectral density of stochastic processes is utilized to differentiate between various types of random motion, such as Brownian motion and Levy flights. This study introduces a streamlined approach to estimate the density of the power spectrum by leveraging the autocorrelation function of a signal's Hilbert transform. This technique is validated using both synthetic data and recordings of mechanical Brownian movement from a cantilever.

This study investigates the conservation of energy in nonhomogeneous flows characterized by vorticity, a density gradient, and an external force field. We establish that for the energy to remain constant, the force field must be conservative, the density field must be barotropic, and a specific condition relating the force field, vorticity, and density gradient must be met. These findings extend earlier research by S. K. Khandekar and S. M. Shahriar.

This paper introduces VIRUP, a visualization software designed to support the creation of novel visual representations. Unlike many data visualization tools, VIRUP prioritizes the development of new visual representations. It enables users to generate custom visual representations through scripting, which can be executed in sequence to render scenes. The software supports both Python scripting and JavaScript, allowing users to create custom visual representations through scripting, which can be executed in sequence to render scenes. The Data Bricks Space Mission offers a free, hands-on learning environment designed to help children aged 10 to15 grasp data concepts and acquire data science skills. The activity features a storyline where participants act as data scientists for the Space Agency, tasked with analyzing data to solve critical challenges. The course is structured into three parts: a storyline-driven introduction, two interactive data science modules, and a final project. The course is currently available on the Code.org platform.

SDN offers a promising method for managing network traffic, yet it is susceptible to implementation flaws that can cause flow tables to deviate from their intended designs. Consequently, verifying flow table accuracy is essential to ensure network traffic adheres to the programmed policies. This paper introduces a formal verification framework for SDN that translates flow table rules into a set of constraints, then employs an SMT solver to determine if these constraints can be satisfied. By demonstrating the method's application on two specific scenarios, the study illustrates how the proposed approach can effectively detect flow table programming errors.

Generative models are frequently employed to create novel content by modifying existing outputs through latent codes. However, the presence of semantic entanglement within these latent spaces often hinders the ability to make specific alterations. This paper proposes a weak disentanglement strategy designed to facilitate targeted changes in both image-to-image translation and video generation. The approach relies on a new objective function that encourages the model to learn a weaker disentanglement structure, enabling controlled editing of generative models by altering only a few latent dimensions. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness on video generation, specifically by changing the number of people depicted in scenes. Additionally, the proposed technique is applied to image-to-image translation, allowing for controlled editing of the number of individuals in an image.

This study examines the aerodynamic performance of a two-dimensional tandem wing configuration, consisting of a leading and a trailing airfoil, through direct numerical simulations. The analysis focuses on the effects of varying the inter-foil gap ($h$) and angle of attack ($\alpha$) on the flow dynamics and overall lift. At a constant Reynolds number of $10^5$, the flow regime is characterized by the presence of strong leading-edge vortices (LEVs) on both airfoils. These LEVs are primarily responsible for the observed lift generation. The flow field is categorized into four distinct regimes based on $h$ and $\alpha$: (1) a low-lift regime where the trailing LEV is weak and unstable; (2) a high-lift regime where the trailing LEV is strong and stable; (3) a high-lift regime where the trailing LEV is strong but unstable; and (4) a low-lift regime where the trailing LEV is weak and unstable. The third regime is further divided into two sub-regimes based on the stability of the trailing LEV. Real-time physics is essential for understanding the dynamics of quantum systems, yet it remains difficult to study due to the non-hermitian nature of real-time evolution. Consequently, extracting spectral functions from Euclidean data via analytic continuation is ill-posed, and existing methods often fail to adequately address these challenges. This study introduces a novel approach that employs a deep generative model to address these hurdles. By utilizing a variational autoencoder, we first learn a low-dimensional latent representation of Euclidean two-point functions. We then condition this representation on a proposed prior distribution to generate the spectral function. This method is validated using synthetic data and tested against lattice QCD gluon spectral functions.

A quantum dot can serve as a probe for the addition spectrum of a superconductor by acting as a reference for the chemical potential of a superconducting reservoir. This approach enables the investigation of unconventional superconductors, including those with non-trivial pairing symmetries, topological superconductors, and those exhibiting non-equilibrium states. We examine the feasibility of utilizing a quantum dot to detect signatures of topological superconductivity in superconducting materials. This detection relies on observing a specific set of conductance peaks within a differential conductance spectrum. These peaks emerge from the interplay between the quantudot and the superconducting environment, occurring when the latter possesses a chiral Majorana edge mode. Our analysis indicates that these peaks are robust against variations in the system's parameters.

The growing demand for new pharmaceuticals has driven the adoption of computational methods to design molecules, a process that benefits significantly from generative techniques. These methods, capable of creating novel structures based on existing chemical data, are particularly effective for molecules with specific properties, such as drugs. This paper introduces a new framework for generating candidate drug molecules by integrating a deep generative model with a reinforcement learning (RL) agent. The system utilizes a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) to learn the latent distribution of drug molecules, enabling the sampling of new chemical structures. A specific CVAE architecture is designed to generate valid molecules by conditioning the sampling process on chemical substructures. This learned distribution guides the RL agent, which then refines these generated structures to optimize target properties. The proposed method was evaluated using a dataset of 1,000 drug molecules, where it successfully produced new candidates with improved performance compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

We present the Dynamic GoI Machine (DGoIM), a fresh abstract machine for $\lambda_{\bot}$ that functions as a dynamic variant of Goard's GoI Machine. Within Accattoli's classification scheme for abstract machines in the $\lambda_{\bot}$ calculus, DGoIM occupies the position of a "stack machine with a register." This designation signifies that DGoIM combines the defining traits of both stack machines and register machines. Specifically, it operates as a stack machine by utilizing a call stack for managing recursive abstractions, while employing a register to store the argument against which reduction occurs.

This study introduces a machine learning framework designed to analyze the stellar populations of the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) by leveraging data from the Gaia-ESO Survey (GES). The approach utilizes GES spectroscopic observations alongside photometric data from the Pan-STARRS1 3-Gyr survey. We employ a novel technique that integrates a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a random forest (RF) algorithm to classify LMC stars into their respective evolutionary stages. The CNN learns to identify spectral features, while the RF algorithm maps these learned features to specific evolutionary categories. The model's performance is validated using GES spectra, achieving an accuracy of 97.4% for main sequence stars and 94.2% for red giant branch stars. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the CNN's learned features can effectively distinguish between LMC and Milky Way stars, achieving a classification accuracy of 99.9%. This methodology offers a robust tool for analyzing stellar populations in the LMC and other external galaxies using Pan-STARRS1 photometry combined with GES spectra.

This paper introduces a novel approach to identifying electricity theft by leveraging the time-series characteristics of data. The proposed method utilizes a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to forecast energy usage based on historical patterns. The discrepancy between these predictions and the recorded actual meter readings serves as the metric for detecting theft. The model's efficacy is demonstrated using real-world data from the Brazilian distribution utility company, Enel Distribuidora Rio de Janeiro.

This paper investigates sparse and tight graphs embedded on surfaces, specifically analyzing their base graphs. For the torus, we have identified 19 distinct irreducible base graphs. Furthermore, we have computed the enumeration of sparse and tight graphs for the torus, as well as for the sphere and projective plane with up to 12 vertices.

The LHCb experiment has determined the $\Lambda^0_c$ baryon lifetime by analyzing $\Xi^0_c\to K^-\pi^+$ decays, where the $\Xi^0_c$ is reconstructed via its $\Lambda^0\to p\pi^-$ decay chain. The analysis utilizes an integrated luminosity of 3.0 fb$^{-1}$ collected at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV. The resulting measured lifetime is $(20.3\pm 0.8\pm 1.0)$ ps, which aligns with the prior LHCb measurement. The first uncertainty reflects statistical precision, while the second accounts for systematic effects.

Sparse Subspace Clustering (SSC) is a prevalent unsupervised learning technique for segmenting data into clusters. Although SSC offers strong performance, it suffers from high computational costs and fails to utilize spatial information, which is critical in image segmentation tasks. This paper introduces a new algorithm that addresses these limitations by integrating SSC with a Graph Cut method. Our approach employs SSC to generate initial cluster labels and subsequently refines these labels by exploiting the spatial characteristics of the images. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms existing SSC-based algorithms in both efficiency and segmentation quality.

Melt ponds are a crucial component of the Arctic system, significantly altering the surface energy balance and influencing the broader climate. This study introduces a new parameterization designed to integrate melt pond dynamics into the Community Earth System Model (CESM). The approach utilizes a two-layer ice model, where the upper layer represents the ice surface and the lower layer acts as an effective medium representing the rest of the ice structure. The interaction between sunlight and the ice surface is governed by a two-stream radiative transfer model, which calculates the spatial distribution of melt pond area and depth. These parameters are updated daily using a mass balance scheme that accounts for solar heating, evaporation, and refreezing. The model was evaluated against observational data from the 2012 and 2014 melt seasons, demonstrating strong agreement with measurements of ice albedo, melt pond area, and surface temperatures. CESM simulations indicate that melt pond formation increases the surface energy flux by 15% to 20%, thereby accelerating ice melting. Furthermore, the model predicts that Arctic sea ice volume will decrease by approximately 10% by 2100 under a high-emission scenario, assuming melt pond development is included in the simulation.

We demonstrate that changing the transition to a specific target final spin projection during atom-molecule scattering can be mitigated by employing a Feshbach resonance. We present a straightforward physical explanation for this phenomenon, which is then validated through numerical calculations.

This study demonstrates the link between the probability density function (PDF) of the displacement in correlated anomalous diffusion and the central limit theorem's convergence to $q$-Gaussian distributions within the framework of fractional calculus. We establish that these $q$-Gaussian distributions are intrinsically tied to the emergence of correlated anomalous diffusion, and utilizing the properties of the Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative, we derive the specific value of the Gell-Mann-Qiao parameter $q$ associated with this process.

We introduce a novel mechanism for tuning the characteristics of Weyl nodes and surface Fermi arcs within higher-order nodal line semimetals. This approach relies on the inherent momentum-space symmetry of such materials, which permits the manipulation of surface Fermi arc trajectories through the backgate-induced shift of bulk valence band edges. Consequently, this technique enables the creation of both gapped and gapless Fermi arcs. Furthermore, we identify a specific condition for inducing a bandgap in the nodal line and outline the resulting evolution of Fermi arcs during such a topological phase transition.

This study introduces a reputation management protocol designed for the decentralized cloud computing environment of the Helix network. In Helix, every node possesses a reputation score that influences its likelihood of being selected for tasks. The proposed mechanism estimates a node's trustworthiness by analyzing the success rate of its past assignments. Additionally, it incorporates a dynamic approach to adjust reputation values, ensuring that nodes with poor performance are penalized while those executing tasks correctly are rewarded.

This study introduces a novel linear perceptual quality assessment for point clouds, designed to evaluate the fidelity of 3D data after compression. The core methodology involves projecting point clouds onto multiple views and applying a 2D linear quality metric to each perspective. We demonstrate that this approach achieves superior correlation with subjective quality scores compared to existing objective measures. Furthermore, the model's effectiveness is validated through an ablation study, which confirms that each viewpoint uniquely captures specific visual attributes.

We examine the Hawking-Page phase transition within the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence, which links transitions in bulk black hole spacetimes to quarkyonic transitions occurring in the dual QCD theory on the boundary. This study involves a holographic model of QCD that incorporates the backreaction of fundamental matter fields on the geometry. We demonstrate that the inclusion of this backreaction enables the simultaneous description of black hole phase transitions and the dual quarkyonic transitions. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of the backreaction on thermodynamic properties, including the Helmholtz free energy, entropy, and specific heat.

This study introduces a novel, self-supervised deep learning framework designed to classify knee MRI scans for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) and medial collateral ligament (MCL) tears. The method involves segmenting the ligaments and applying contrastive learning to the resulting slices. Experimental results indicate that this approach is highly effective, achieving an accuracy of 90.4% on the internal test set and 89.5% on the external test set. Furthermore, the framework demonstrates robust generalization capabilities, successfully adapting to data from other institutions and MRI scanners.

This study introduces a new font generation method that creates stylistic variations for existing fonts by leveraging a cross-attention mechanism to integrate style information into the content glyphs. The system is designed to produce high-quality, readable output that accurately reflects the input style, even when the original font lacks specific character structures (such as periods or question marks) or contains typographical errors. The content and style inputs are processed through separate pathways, with style features propagated to the content via cross-attention. The approach was tested on a dataset comprising 1,000 words and 1,000 styles, with evaluations focusing on character-level accuracy, overall string readability, and the quality of the generated style. This study examines the covariant formulation of a charged fluid within a spacetime characterized by torsion, utilizing the Einstein-Cartan-Kirchhoff framework. The analysis focuses on the evolution of the charged fluid, deriving its covariant energy-momentum tensor and establishing the corresponding equations of motion. The results demonstrate that torsion influences the energy-momentum tensor only through the spin density; it does not alter the kinematic properties of the fluid, nor does it introduce new terms into the equations of motion.

This study introduces a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework designed to optimize video streaming quality of experience (QoE) by intelligently selecting streaming parameters. The proposed DRL agent dynamically adapts to fluctuating network conditions and user preferences to maximize QoE, while simultaneously adhering to constraints regarding computational resources and buffering. To achieve this, we developed a novel streaming model that integrates adaptive bitrate (ABR) selection with buffer management. The agent employs a deep Q-network (DQN) to learn an optimal policy for choosing streaming actions. This study presents measurements of the $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ production cross-sections in the mid-rapidity region ($|y|<0.3$) for central $pp$ and $p\text{-}p\text{-}\text{Pb}$ collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\text{NN}}}=5.02$ TeV. The analysis focuses on the $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ transverse momentum ($p_{\text{T}}$) distributions, as well as the $p_{\text{T}}$ spectra of $J/\psi$ states within the $0<p_{\text{T}}<8$ GeV/$c$ range. Additionally, the $p_{\text{T}}$ distributions for $J/\psi$ states are examined in relation to charged-particle multiplicity. The study also evaluates the $p_{\text{T}}$ spectra of $J/\psi$ states within the $p\text{-}p\text{-}\text{Pb}$ context, comparing them to $pp$ data and exploring the $p_{\text{T}}$ dependence of the $J/\psi$ nuclear modification factor, $R_{\text{-}\text{-}\text{-}\text{-}\text{-}\text{-}\text{-}\text{-}\text{-}\text{-}\text{-}\text{-}\text{-}\text{-}\text

We introduce a streamlined and versatile protocol for determining the entropy of spin-1/2 systems, applicable to both thermal equilibrium and non-equilibrium states. This approach offers a significant advantage over prior techniques by eliminating the necessity for complete knowledge of the system's Hamiltonian. We validate the protocol through numerical simulations of a thermal equilibrium Ising model and through experiments on a trapped ion platform, successfully quantifying the entropy generated by a quantum quench in the same experimental setup.

This study establishes the Geometric Modulus Principle, which serves as a foundational tool for deriving numerous classical results in analysis through compact arguments. We demonstrate that the modulus of a family of curves corresponds to a specific class of subadditive set functions defined on an associated ring of sets. Leveraging this framework, we reprove several fundamental theorems—including the Five Point Theorem, the Lusin E Theorem, and the Riesz Representation Theorem for Borel measures—offering fresh perspectives grounded in geometric and functional analysis.

This study examines the discrete Schrödinger equation featuring both near- and long-range interactions. We establish that the longest-range forces prevent soliton collapse, whereas short-range forces permit it. By analyzing the behavior of the equation near the singular regime, we derive an asymptotic formula for the sequence of solutions.

This method is widely used in various engineering applications, such as structural optimization and the design of complex systems. However, it is a non-convex problem, which makes it difficult to solve using standard optimization algorithms. The Multiparametric (MM) algorithm is a powerful method for solving non-convex problems by iteratively approximating the objective function with a sequence of convex problems. The MM algorithm has been successfully applied to a wide range of problems, including those in signal processing, control theory, and machine learning. In this paper, we present a novel application of the MM algorithm to solve signomial programming problems. We introduce a technique for generating 3D avatars from video sequences that explicitly accounts for incomplete and noisy depth data. This approach employs a novel depth-aware autoencoder, which learns to reconstruct missing portions of avatars from partial geometry, effectively mitigating artifacts caused by inaccurate depth measurements. Additionally, the system incorporates a shape refinement module that leverages the speaker's 3D facial structure to optimize avatar quality. Empirical results demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches in both visual fidelity and shape accuracy.

Face reconstruction from a single image has emerged as a significant challenge in computer vision, with recent deep learning advancements demonstrating remarkable success. Nevertheless, most current approaches rely on the assumption that input images are fully frontal and well-lit, conditions that are rarely met in real-world scenarios. To address this limitation, we introduce a new framework for face reconstruction that explicitly accounts for challenging conditions such as partial occlusion and non-frontal poses. Our approach leverages 3D morphable models (3DMMs) to synthesize missing facial regions, while simultaneously deriving 2D pose and illumination parameters from the input image. We have developed a specialized network for estimating these parameters and trained a new 3DMM using a large-scale dataset. Experimental results indicate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in de-occluding faces and effectively reconstructs faces from difficult inputs.

Intrinsically motivated reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising pathway to address the challenges of deep RL in complex, high-dimensional environments. By substituting extrinsic rewards with internal, hierarchically organized goals, this approach enables RL agents to engage in activities that lack immediate utility for their overarching objective. Current methods, however, often rely on heuristic designs for these internal objectives, whereas intrinsically-motivated RL is intended to be self-directed. This study introduces a novel, self-driven strategy for exploring intrinsically motivated RL. We demonstrate that within the context of the Hopper environment, this new method surpasses both standard RL and various heuristic-driven intrinsically motivated RL frameworks.

This study examines a distributed approach to solving the linear quadratic (LQ) problem within a network of agents, where each agent optimizes its own local cost function. We introduce a novel Localized Policy Iteration (LPI) algorithm that leverages the augmented system framework to determine optimal local control policies. By analyzing the optimality gap between LPI's iterates and the globally optimal solution, we demonstrate that this gap diminishes as the neighborhood size (denoted as $N$) increases. Furthermore, we establish a bound on the convergence rate of the LPI algorithm, showing that its performance degrades polynomially with respect to $1/N$. We also derive a lower bound on the convergence rate gap, proving that it scales polynomially with the local cost function dimension ($m$). Finally, numerical simulations validate our theoretical findings and illustrate the trade-off between computational complexity and convergence speed.

This study examines the characteristics of events devoid of charged particles, a category that is notably scarce in standard Monte Carlo simulations which typically assume exclusive color-singlet exchange. By analyzing data from the UA2 experiment at the CERN Sp$ arpcollider$ (900 GeV center-of-mass energy), we observe that the frequency of these events aligns well with predictions derived from models including both single-particle and multi-particle color-singlet exchange mechanisms.

The electronic band structure of penta-silicene is highly tunable through external electric fields, rendering it a highly promising candidate for both thermoelectric and photovoltaic applications. This study investigates the impact of a monolayer of penta-silicene placed in contact with a Au(111) substrate on its electronic properties. We find that the penta-silicene layer undergoes a significant band structure transformation, evolving from a semimetal to a semiconductor with a band gap of approximately 0.3 eV. This shift is driven by the breaking of the pita-silicene's inversion symmetry caused by the substrate and the resulting electronic charge transfer. Furthermore, we explore the effects of various surface defects on the pitaoual layer's electronic properties. Our results indicate that the pitaoual layer is remarkably robust against defects, with the band structure remaining largely unaffected even when the pitaoual layer is penetrated by the defects. This suggests that the pitaoual layer is an ideal candidate for use as a van der Waals heterostructure with gold.

This study examines the thermal dissociation of bottom quarkonium within a fractional hot medium, utilizing the AdS/CFT correspondence and AdS space with a fractional dimension. The analysis focuses on the quark-antiquark potential's screening length, determining the thermal dissociation temperature for bottomonia. Results indicate that the screening length diminishes as the fractional parameter rises, consequently causing the decomposition temperature of bottom quarkonium to increase.

Historical collisions between Earth and dark matter subhalos could have left physical traces in geological materials. We examine the potential for detecting such encounters by analyzing the distribution of subhalo masses and densities, which are derived from the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model. Our analysis reveals that, within this framework, the mass density distribution of subhalos follows a power law with an exponent of approximately $-2.2$. This specific slope aligns with the maximum mass that a subhalo can possess before merging with its host galaxy, a limit determined by the galaxy's mass and the subhalo's initial mass. Consequently, the mass density distribution of subhalos is largely independent of the galaxy's mass. We further demonstrate that the mass density distribution of subhalos is relatively insensitive to the formation time of the galaxy, provided the galaxy's mass exceeds the mass of the subhalo. These findings suggest that the mass density distribution of subhalos is primarily determined by the galaxy's mass and the subhalo's initial mass, rather than by the galaxy's mass and formation time.

This paper investigates coordinated patrolling in a network of locations by a team of agents, where each robot's movement is governed by a Poisson process. We introduce a novel framework for formulating a decentralized, multi-agent patrol problem that accounts for uncertainties in both agent movement dynamics and location visitation frequencies. Specifically, we model the patrolling decision as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and integrate an uncertainty metric into the objective function to balance exploration and exploitation. Our primary contribution is a novel decentralized reinforcement learning approach that employs a two-layered structure: a central layer for training a shared policy across agents, and a local layer for executing that policy. We demonstrate that this method is provably effective in generating a Poisson process that optimizes the patrol objective. Furthermore, we validate the approach through simulations on a two-agent system, showing that incorporating uncertainty significantly enhances decision-making quality. Finally, we establish a lower bound on the convergence rate of our proposed learning algorithm.

This paper introduces a new framework for robot navigation that integrates deep reinforcement learning (DRL) with a specialized path planning component. Our method achieves superior success rates and higher-quality trajectories compared to existing approaches. To further enhance performance, we developed a novel training strategy that leverages a pre-trained model to adapt to new environments. This transfer learning technique significantly boosts the efficiency of training and generalization. Extensive testing across 100 distinct environments demonstrates that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, delivering faster training times, greater generalization capabilities, and improved performance.

This study examines the magnetic phase diagram of a dipole ensemble situated on a face-centered cubic (FCC) lattice. The model incorporates both nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor dipole-dipole interactions, alongside a uniform magnetic field. The phase diagram is divided into distinct regions based on the ground state configurations of these dipoles. The analysis reveals that the system exhibits complex magnetic behaviors, including magnetic ordering, frustration, and disorder. The results are compared with those of a theoretical model that accounts solely for nearest-neighbor dipole-dipole interactions.

This study demonstrates that it is possible to uniquely determine a homogeneous inclusion with constant conductivity within a bounded domain, along with its location and orientation, using only external measurements. This reconstruction is achievable through a newly introduced method for solving the inverse problem associated with harmonic measure.

This study examines the stability of axisymmetric magnetic fields within a slowly rotating, rotating star, focusing on the interplay between toroidal and poloidal components. Our findings indicate that these components can mutually stabilize one another, a phenomenon that persists even when accounting for slow rotation. Specifically, a toroidal field can stabilize a poloidal field, and vice versa. Furthermore, we analyze the stability of a magnetic field with a mixed poloidal-toroidal configuration. Our analysis reveals that while a toroidal magnetic field can stabilize against dynamo instability, a purely poloidal magnetic field remains susceptible to dynamo action.

The Kuramoto model serves as a foundational framework for analyzing synchronization in complex, interconnected systems. While originally formulated as a second-order system of differential equations, it has been extended to higher-order variants, which incorporate additional dynamics to account for phenomena like phase-locked states and multi-cluster synchronization. This study examines the higher-order Kuramoto model within the context of simplicial topology, a framework that extends graph theory to include higher-dimensional interactions. We demonstrate that both the dynamics and the synchronization properties of this model are significantly influenced by simplicial topology. Furthermore, we derive a consensus protocol for the higher-order Kuramoto model that functions effectively on simplicial complexes.

Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) is a critical operation in scientific computing, yet its performance heavily relies on the specific matrix being processed. To optimize SpMV across diverse hardware, one must identify the most effective memory layout and the most efficient execution algorithm. This paper presents a comprehensive benchmarking suite designed to evaluate SpMV algorithms and memory layouts, capable of analyzing hundreds of matrices across various architectures. The suite employs a multi-threaded, multi-lane design that utilizes OpenMP for thread-level parallelism and CUDA for GPU acceleration. The benchmarking methodology is detailed alongside performance results from extensive tests conducted on a large set of matrices spanning various sparsity patterns and sizes, executed on both CPU and GPU systems.

This study investigates the normality of a family of meromorphic functions that share several points with partial sharing from a normal family of similar functions. We demonstrate that within this framework, the number of shared points and the nature of their sharing are not critical, as we establish a theorem linking these concepts. Furthermore, we present examples showing that sharing points with a normal family does not necessarily imply the non-normality of a related family.

Accurate detection of a robot operator's intent is crucial for enabling safe and effective human-robot collaboration (HRC). However, current methods often rely on complex sensors and data processing, limiting their practical application in real-world settings. This study introduces a simplified approach to intention recognition that utilizes only the robot's existing kinematic data. By employing a straightforward linear regression model, the proposed method generates a trajectory prediction that serves as the basis for intent assessment. This framework is designed to handle both static and dynamic intents, specifically targeting the recognition of movement versus stopping. Experimental results demonstrate that this technique achieves an intention recognition accuracy of 80.5%, confirming that significant prediction precision can be maintained even with reduced technological complexity.

This study demonstrates that homogeneous Monge-Ampère systems are linked to flat hyperspherical, hyperbolic, and de Spherical geometries. Specifically, within spherical geometry, these systems define pairs of orthogonal (Lagrangian) complex affine subspaces; in hyperbolic geometry, they correspond to pairs of orthogonal (Lagangrian) complex hyperplanes; and in de Spherical geometry, they map to pairs of orthogonal (Lagangrian) real affine subspaces.

This study examines the behavior of gas bubbles in an electrolytic cell, specifically focusing on the influence of solutal natural convection. A two-dimensional numerical model was developed to simulate the dynamics of a single bubble and the associated concentration fields. The analysis covers the entire bubble lifecycle, from nucleation to detachment, within a simplified electrolytic cell. Results indicate that solutally-induced natural convection significantly influences bubble behavior, a finding that holds substantial relevance for industrial-scale applications.

This study examines the potential for discovering supersymmetry in the context of long-lived neutralinos, which decay into a pair of charginos within the detector. The proposed analysis utilizes a dataset from the 2016 CMS proton-proton collision experiment at the LHC, recorded at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. The event selection targets signatures characterized by significant missing transverse energy alongside two or three isolated leptons. The analysis results indicate no statistically significant excess over the Standard Model background predictions. Consequently, the findings are used to derive upper limits on the production cross-sections of neutralinos with proper decay lengths ranging from 0.1 mm to 100 meters. The mass exclusion limits for neutralinos are shown to be sensitive to their lifetime, with the exclusion bounds tightening for longer lifetimes.

This study examines how the specific heat of Dirac semimetals responds to the violation of full rotational symmetry, which alters the Fermi surface from circular to elliptical. While the specific heat of ideal two-dimensional Dirac fermions exhibits linear temperature dependence, the elliptical distortion introduces an additional term proportional to the square of the temperature. This secondary term becomes dominant at sufficiently high temperatures.

This work proposes a novel ASP-based methodology for converting sequential code into concurrent programs. We demonstrate that ASP can effectively model the intricate, multi-step transformation rules of GraftJS, a popular JavaScript concurrency library, by encoding these rules within an ASP solver. The resulting program generates concrete concurrent code structures from an existing sequential input.

We present a novel torsion pendulum setup designed to detect the gravitational pull from objects with masses as low as 100 nanograms. The experiment utilizes a 100 nanogram test mass positioned 2.5 millimeters above the center of a 20-microgram pendulum with a 20-millimeter span. By integrating this configuration with a capacitance-differential readout system, we aim to achieve a sensitivity of 200 attometers per square root of the integration time. The paper details the experimental arrangement, initial results, and the projected sensitivity limits.

CCH serves as a crucial probe for detecting the CCH/CN ratio in the interstellar medium, a key indicator of the chemical equilibrium between the HACA and FCH mechanisms. This study reports the first detection of CCH toward the protostar IRAS 16547-2487, alongside the first identification of the CN isotope CN-13N in the hot core of IRAS 16547-2487. The CCH/derivative(CN) abundance ratio for the hot core is approximately 0.01, a value roughly ten times lower than that observed in the hot corinos of the same source. This discrepancy suggests that the CCH/CN ratio in the hot core is significantly more chemically equilibrated than in the hot corinos. Furthermore, the CCH/derivative(CN) ratio for the hot core is about a factor of 100 lower than that of the hot corinos, indicating that the CCH/CN ratio in the hot corinos is less equilibrated than in the hot core.

We introduce a new framework for asymmetric dark matter that links baryogenesis with the asymmetry of the dark sector. This model features a singlet scalar field that couples to Standard Model particles and a complex scalar field that remains singlet under the Standard Model but interacts with the first. During the electroweak epoch, the interaction between these fields generates a non-zero imaginary component in the mass of the first field, triggering baryon asymmetry. Crucially, the mechanism relies on a non-thermal production of the scalar fields, which allows the model to satisfy current cosmological observations. Additionally, the framework predicts a viable mass scale for asymmetric dark matter and offers a distinct signature for dark matter detection through direct observation.

This study presents a measurement of the $t\bar{t}Z$ process cross section using proton-proton collision data at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, recorded by the CMS detector at the LHC. The analysis utilizes an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$, with final states containing a $b$-tagged $W$ boson, a top quark, and a $Z$ boson. The observed cross section aligns with Standard Model predictions within a 10% margin, while the $t\bar{Z}$ production rate is determined to be 1.5 times more prevalent than the $t\bar{Z}$ channel.

This investigation focuses on the connections between black hole moduli spaces and symplectic group orbits, specifically the symplectic and Kr\"{u}ller-Suslin group orbits, within the context of the STU model. This paper explores the relationships between the moduli spaces of black holes and the orbits of the STU model.
